html:
The Muckleshoot are a Coast Salish people of the Green and White river valleys of western Washington, southeast of Seattle. Their name comes from a prairie in the area, and they speak Lushootseed.

Before 1855 there was no single Muckleshoot tribe. Several village peoples lived along these rivers, fishing for salmon and hunting in the foothills of the Cascades. After the treaties of Medicine Creek (1854) and Point Elliott (1855) and the Puget Sound War that followed, the Muckleshoot Reservation was set up in 1857 for people of these upriver villages, among them Duwamish and upper Puyallup groups. The Muckleshoot Indian Tribe formed its government in 1936. Its members have defended treaty fishing rights in the courts, part of the fight that led to the Boldt Decision of 1974.
